question.problem:
If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $\text{Col}(A-3I)={R}^{3}$

II. $A-3I$ is singular

III. $\lambda =3$ is an eigenvalue of $A$
question.worked_solution:
Given a $3\times 3$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=3=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $M$ has $3$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(M)+\text{nullity}(M)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. According to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A-3I) & =3-\text{nullity}(A-3I) \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

According to invertible matrix theorem, $\text{Col}(A-3I)={R}^{3}.$

- Statements II is false. By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A-3I)=0,$ we obtain that $A-3I$ must be non-singular.

- Statement III is false. Notice that if $M=A-3I$ is non-singular, then $(A-3I)x=0$ has only zero solution. As a result, $\lambda =3$ can not be an eigenvalue of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
